specs and the components. And as cars become more appliance-like, there is really nothing separating
them from the same fate. Which leads us neatly onto the China problem. We briefly touched on it,
but Chinese EVs and hybrids are here and their cost to performance ratio is very hard to compete
with. Now, in America, this hasn't mattered yet because trade barriers keep us isolated to the
point that we really do live in our own little car bubble. A lot of the most popular cars in
North America simply don't exist outside of North America. Seeing an F-150 in Europe, for example,
is extremely rare. This is either because our cars are too large for roads in other major
markets of Europe and Asia, too inefficient for local laws, or because there are just better,
cheaper local alternatives. Now, that's typically been fine for us at least, because the USA is such
a large market that even foreign automakers set up operations here to get inside the
bubble. But there are a lot of manufacturers, particularly those from Europe and Japan,
that depend far more heavily on exporting cars beyond their home country. And for a long time,
the single largest and fastest growing market was China itself. European automakers in particular
enjoyed several years of selling high-end cars to status-driven consumers in the rapidly developing
Chinese economy. And for most of that time, they really didn't have any competition because locally
produced Chinese cars were almost embarrassingly cheap, poorly engineered, lacking in features,
and most importantly, they couldn't compete with the status of the European luxury brands.
But that has clearly changed. Even despite being largely protected from Chinese competition on
their home turf, European automakers have run into a serious problem trying to sell their cars
into China because local alternatives are now far more competitive. Xiaomi,
a company that didn't even have a car division 5 years ago, delivered over 400,000 vehicles in its
first full year of making cars. And the base model outsold the Tesla Model 3 in China in 2025. And on
the point of badge engineering again, a Porsche Tekcon is still more of a status symbol than a
Xiaomi SU7 despite looking almost identical. But in some cases, that's actually working against
the European automakers. Just like Americans like to buy American cars, a level of nationalism is
pushing some Chinese consumers to buy Chinese cars. Even before considering their exports,
the rise of Chinese automakers have hurt the incumbent players that are losing one of their
most valuable markets. But well, it would also be irresponsible not to include their exports
because they are coming. According to data from the Rodeium Group, China exported over 1
million vehicles to the EU in 2025, accounting for around 6 to 7% of the market. And in early 2026,
those exports accelerated by 62% yearonear. BYD alone delivered 2.6 million vehicles last year,
commanding roughly 20% of the global EV market. Australia is actually a really interesting case
study here because they are a nice little guinea pig for the larger American market given some
important similarities. Big roads, consumers with strong purchasing power and a surface
level cultural similarity to America. But because they no longer have a local car industry, Chinese
manufacturers are treated the same as every other manufacturer and they are dominating because of
their cost competitiveness. Now, of course, there is the argument that China has subsidized these
auto manufacturers to make them as competitive as they are today through co-investment and
vertically integrated industrial planning. This is absolutely true, but it's also only fair to point
out that American and European automakers are also the beneficiaries of generous government policy.
And for what it's worth, China has also let a lot of their EV manufacturers fail. China has actually
let more EV companies fail than America has had automakers in its entire history. We are now just
seeing the ones that have actually survived. Now, all of these problems would be a serious threat to
a healthy car market. But the fourth big problem is that over the next few years in particular,
a wall of debt is likely to mean they are fighting for a smaller slice of a smaller pie. Now, we all
know people are spending irresponsible money every month so they can drive a car they can't
reasonably afford. But there is one big piece of this that often gets ignored. We are about to
hit peak refinance. The average transaction price for a new vehicle in America has gone from around
$38,000 in 2019 to just under $49,000 today. And a lot of the car loans from the cheap money
era are now expiring. Loans that were written when interest rates were near zero and monthly
repayments were a lot more manageable. This means if people want to upgrade into a similar vehicle,
they are going to be paying a higher interest rate on a higher base price, making deals significantly
harder to do. According to data from Lending Tree, the average monthly payment on a new vehicle hit
$773 in the first quarter of 2026, and one in five buyers now commits to a payment of
$1,000 or more each month. Of course, people will pay irresponsible amounts, but there are still
fundamental limits to what loans can be given with any hope of repayment. Another underappreciated
factor is that these financing realities are just making newer, more expensive vehicles harder to
sell. Again, people will sign up for some pretty irresponsible lending if they see they are getting
themselves into a better car. But, as we saw earlier, car features that most people care
about have pretty much plateaued while prices and interest rates have increased. Higher repayments
for a downgrade, even if it is just the trim level, is a lot harder to get people excited about
at a dealership negotiating table. The industry's uh solution to this has basically been to just
make the loans longer. Effective loan terms after refinancing now average over 90 months, or 7 1/2
years of repayment on a depreciating asset. In January 2026, the 60-day delinquency rate on
subprime auto loans hit 6.9%. the highest level recorded in more than three decades of tracking.
And roughly 31% of trade-ins towards new vehicles now carry negative equity with the average
underwater amount sitting at around $7,200. EVs in particular are now depreciating faster than their
internal combustion engine equivalent, averaging around 58 to 59% depreciation over 5 years
compared to roughly 45 to 46% for IC. And beyond that, cars are statistically lasting longer,
too. So, it's harder to make a new deal happen while also easier to just keep driving the same
vehicle for longer, which for what it's worth is exactly what people should be doing as long as
it's still safe. People can't afford to trade up and the cars they're sitting in are in many cases
just as well equipped as anything they would be able to trade into with the same repayment. The
final thing is that higher interest rates are also hurting manufacturers themselves just as much as
their customers. Most large auto manufacturers carry a lot of debt to finance their financing
divisions, but also to fund their ongoing, highly capital-intensive operation. Ford, for example,
has closed $163 billion worth of debt on their books, with 22 billion of that being for their
core business functions. Just the interest on that debt now accounts for as much as half of their
free cash flow. Now, individually, these are all problems that car manufacturers are worried about,
but together it is a bit of a perfect storm. Companies are burning capital they are running
out of for products their customers are struggling to afford in a market that is
getting more competitive and harder to stand out in. It sounds bad, but it gets worse. This
is just what has been happening recently. So, if you want the full breakdown, go and watch

has one of the highest rates of upward mobility of any metro area in the country. A child born
in the bottom fifth of the income distribution in San Jose, has a 12.9% chance of reaching the
top fifth by the age of 30. In Charlotte, North Carolina, that number is just 4.4%. Additionally,
for what it's worth, the top fifth of income earners in San Jose are also on average taking
home a lot more. So, Silicon Valley is already seen as one of the last places where the economic
ladder still kind of works, which makes the people living there or more likely moving there
especially receptive to the idea that time for up or out is coming to an end. For a long time, this
was the place where smart people could come and earn truly life-changing amounts of money. even if
they didn't come from a wealthy background. Tech was arguably even more meritocratic than finance
or big law or medicine, which all had their own gatekeeping mechanisms that favored people from
the right schools or the right families. And a lot of the people who moved here had a similar plan.
Work hard, save aggressively, vest some shares, and get out before you burn out. Now, I know
this is a generalization and things have changed recently, but for a long time, tech in particular
also promoted a less ostentatious lifestyle than a similar high-end career in finance or law. People
were earning genuinely ridiculous money in the valley and still wearing company hoodies while
primarily getting their entertainment from going on hikes and playing video games. Instead of
buying ludicrously expensive housing, the culture of Silicon Valley workers was more paired back and
focus on just watching number go up in their vesting and brokerage accounts. I know it's
anecdotal and I personally didn't work in tech, but when I lived and worked in San Francisco,
I had three roommates who did work in tech and were all making more than enough money to live
an extremely comfortable lifestyle anywhere else in the world. But the housing situation and the
save everything you can culture in the area meant that we were all living between three
bedrooms and one bathroom. And this kind of arrangement was considered completely normal.
Someone spending all of their money to live in the valley, even if they could comfortably afford it,
would be genuinely unusual. Again, at least in my own experience, they were doing this because
most of them had a plan to make money and get out. Financial independence was already really popular
amongst tech workers. The idea being save enough, invest everything, build a portfolio large enough
that you can live off the returns permanently, and then go do whatever you actually want to do
with your life. The math behind it is pretty simple. A study from the 1990s found that if
you withdraw about 4% of a diversified portfolio each year, it should last you indefinitely. So, if
your annual expenses are $100,000, you need $2.5 million invested. At $200,000 a year, you need
$5 million. The target is 25 times your annual spending. Now, for most Americans, saving $2.5
million is a fantasy. The median household income is around $80,000. After taxes, housing, food,
transportation, and the average $39,633 in student loan debt, there's not a lot left over. But for
a senior software engineer in San Jose making $400,000 a year at a company that also gives them
restricted stock units that have been appreciating at 30% annually, it was clearly possible. And for
a lot of people who came from humble backgrounds, it really was just one of the last escape hatches
left to financial security. Even for the people that didn't want to go and retire on a ranch in
Colorado at the age of 35, a lot of techworking culture is still built around getting experience
and saving up what is charmingly known as you money. The idea is that once you have this,
you can leave the big companies and go work for a startup or start your own business without being
destitute in the very likely scenario that it doesn't work out. So yeah, already before the
whole AI fear andor hype cycle came around, tech bros were already fully on board with the idea of
jumping social classes. Additionally, this idea of living off your investment to either live a
good life or double down into a startup feeds in really naturally to the third reason why tech bros
have become so obsessed with this idea. It's just really good marketing. Sam Alman has said
publicly that AI will create the first oneperson billion-dollar company. He even reportedly has
a betting pool with his CEO friends about what year it will happen. Now, of course, we all know
that Sam Alman would never say something just to hype up his own products. But if this is possible,
it is probably going to happen in the tech sector where valuations are well generous and a single
person isn't going to be constrained by their physical limitations to produce tangible goods
and services. Now, in response to statements like this, people working in this field either don't
believe their own hype, in which case they might want to make as much money as they can before
the bubble implodes, or if they do believe this narrative, then they think that business equity is
about to become a lot more valuable. And this is the perfect time to be going out alone, of which
the first step is gaining some level of financial independence. No matter which way you interpret
the leaders in the space, they are basically just saying don't be poor or get rich and die trying,
depending on what take you prefer. Either way, the nerdy tech bros that we have grown up with are
kind of going through something. The culture in Silicon Valley has noticeably changed over recent
years to become far more serious. It's gone from bean bag chairs and salad bars to 80 hour weeks,
biohacking, and token maxing with a sprinkle of 10x productivity, whatever that means. The threat
of being stuck in the permanent underclass, especially in a time of sweeping layoffs,
is just a great narrative to keep tech workers on their hashtag grind set. So far in 2026,
over 108,000 tech workers have been laid off. That is on top of roughly 122,000 in 2025 and 150,000
in 2024. Companies are naturally framing many of these cuts as AI related restructuring. But
Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in January that AI redundancy washing will be a significant feature
in 2026, which is a polite way of saying that a lot of companies are just using AI as an excuse
to fire people they already wanted to get rid of because it sounds better in investor letters
than we massively overhired post pandemic and are now spending too much on capex. Entry-level
tech job postings specifically have dropped 50% at major tech companies compared to prepandemic
levels. and hiring of new graduates by the 15 largest tech firms has fallen by more than half
according to an analysis by the SF standard. If your employees genuinely believe that the
window for financial security is closing, they are going to work harder, demand less,
and be less likely to push back on that optional weekend deployment. Now, I know this isn't exactly
shocking to anybody that's been watching Silicon Valley for the past 3 years, and it's certainly
not surprising to people actually on the inside, but again, the logical response to this is using
the time that they do have to make sure that they can escape the permanent underclass before
they get smited off the last ladder up. Outwardly, it's also clearly a marketing spin to make their
companies look all powerful. Who wouldn't want to invest in the company that's going to define
permanent halves and have nots, right? If these companies promote the idea that their technology
is going to reshape the social fabric like the steam engine did during the industrial revolution,
it goes a long way to rationalize their extreme investments into this technology, especially as
the industry lines up to take two and a half AI companies through particularly public initial
public offerings this year. And of course, it's worth pointing out that if these listings go well,
the tech workers themselves will probably have everything they need to escape the
underclass for good. So there is something of a perverse incentive to play along. And well, yeah,
this is objectively the most sensible course of action for these people to be taking individually,
but it's still really hard to ignore the irony of escaping the permanent underclass
by riding the investment returns of creating that underclass in the first place. It sounds dumb,
but it's also not anything new. And if you don't believe me, go watch this next video to find out
why tech bros in particular seem to never learn any of the lessons from the works of fiction
they hold so dear. And don't forget to like and subscribe to keep on learning how money works.

punish the perpetrators This narrative would certainly be supported by the outlets publishing these stories too because to be honest outrage sells But it’s not necessarily the case and perhaps the the result of basic corporate structuring taken to the absolute extreme Limited Liability Corporations are legal entities which as their name suggests have Limited Liability What this means is that if a company goes bankrupt the people that have put money into that company cannot lose anymore than the amount they invested This is very important for modern finance because it means that investors can comfortably put money towards risky projects without the fear of loosing their life savings if the company itself goes under You would probably never invest into a company like Tesla in it’s early days if you were liable to loose more than the money you invested into such an risky proposal Now companies are owned by shareholders these shareholders can take one of three forms The first and most obvious is a human person which accountants and lawyers will refer to as a Natural Person so when you hear the phrase natural person think of squishy meat sacks A shareholder can also be another company think of something like warren buffets Berkshire Hathaway which owns hundreds of smaller companies underneath it Finally a trust can also be a shareholder Now trusts are similar to corporations in a lot of ways they are both separate legal entities they can both hold assets and they both have limited liability Now unlike a corporation a trust is much simpler in its operation While a company can do anything from manufacturing phones to building the next generation of spacecraft a trust is simply an entity that holds onto stuff for the benefit of a pre-determined entity the beneficiary and is controlled by another pre-determined entity the Trustee A simple example is that the beneficiary is some millionaire’s son who receives money from his trust fund that daddy set up for him and the Trustee is the person that has to explain to the pampered 35 year old man-child that he is not letting him withdraw a million dollars from his trust to set up a jet ski jousting league If this all sounds confusing so far don’t worry about it because the best way to understand it all is to actually think of all of these different types of entities as building blocks that can be put one on-top of another in almost any combination you could think of Now with that in mind I want to teach you about one of the most robust corporate structures our there Let’s say you are a very successful businessman legitimate or otherwise let’s not ask too many questions just yet You will have your company here making lot’s of profits and generally doing what most regular companies do by providing a marketable good or service The most basic way for you to own this company is just to be the direct shareholder of the operation But if the company is big enough you really don’t want to do that for two reasons The first is that if the company gets sued or goes bankrupt you lose everything Yes it is a separate legal entity so you won’t personally be liable for any of the companies debts but you still loose your business and your income stream Instead what you do is this Put your profitable company down here and create a holding company to own all of the shares in that business You can also put especially valuable business assets like a warehouse or a shopfront in this holding company Now when your business pays a dividend it does not go you you directly it goes to this holding company If the operation business back down here gets sued it doesn’t matter because it doesn’t own anything that valuable it can just declare bankruptcy and a new business can be made under the holding company who owns the warehouse and everything else of value Now if you are asking what happens if the holding company gets sued you are starting to think like a real businessman The thing is this holding company is far less likely to be sued than an actual operating business because it basically doesn’t do anything other than own things It doesn’t enter into contracts it doesn’t employ people it doesn’t create products it doesn’t take on debts it basically doesn’t do anything that could put it in a position where it could be sued So this is great But we are not done yet you want this holding company to in turn be held by a trust That means that when the holding company passes money up it doesn’t go directly to you it goes to this trust which will then in turn pass money onto you Now if you remember the trust fund needs a trustee as in the person that decides when and what the trust fund pays to you the beneficiary For this you set up yet another company this company will itself Now this is starting to look crazy but what does all of this actually do This makes you financially invincible If you actual operating business gets sued and goes bankrupt oh well it owns nothing so you can just start another one a week later If YOU get sued and need to declare bankruptcy that also doesn’t really matter Why Well because on paper you don’t own any assets of value Sure you keep getting money from the trust fund here but you can’t own a trust it’s just a pass-through entity The only shares that you actually personally own are the ones in the trustee company but they are worthless all they do is determine when a trust disbursement is paid and oh by the way even if those shares are taken off you it doesn’t matter anyway because a trust is required by law to payout any cash it has on hand at least once a financial year to stop a situation where a rogue trustee can hold a beneficiaries money hostage All of the things of real value are held in this holding company here in the middle of this corporate structure which means these assets are protected from both sides by what effectively amounts to limited liability corporate meat shields It doesn’t matter if anything that has any chance of going bankrupt actually does because the assets will be safe and sound here in the middle Now there is absolutely nothing wrong with this structure Almost every wealthy person in the world will employ something similar if not identical to protect themselves financially because an unfortunate reality of getting wealthy is getting sued But here is where things get really interesting There is no need for all of these entities to be registered in the same country An American business can be owned by a British holding company which feeds money into a trust set up in Singapore which eventually feeds money to a Russian citizen Of course that’s just a random example and what the Pandora papers discovered was that wealthy people were picking and choosing the countries to set up these businesses in EXTREMELY carefully It’s a common joke amongst international accountants that setting up these structures is kind of like going shopping for everything that you want A bit of banking privacy from Panama low corporate taxes from Ireland and currency stability from France Just snake your corporate structure through all of these jurisdictions and you will walk away with all of these benefits stacked on top of each other Now here are where things start to get a bit grey It is specifically illegal in most countries to set up corporate structures like this with the sole intention of avoiding taxes How a lot of international businesses get around this rule is by saying that there was some other legitimate reason that it needed to be set up amongst so many countries These can include having multiple offices around the world for business functions owning multiple properties in different countries or even wanting to move money from a country of operation to a country of residence If an American investor owned a coal mine in Brazil there is no problem with them having a Brazilian company owned by an American holding company Deciding what international corporate structures are built for legitimate purposes and what structures are built for illegitimate purposes is where it gets difficult Some jurisdictions have more registered corporations than citizens so auditing every single last one of them is just not feasible Even if it was the guilty parties could very easily get around this issue by having a string of multiple company is set up in a place like Montenegro then the Singaporean financial authorities are likely to just get told to go duck themselves because local laws mean that kind of information is kept secret You can start to see the problem here and you can start to see why these data leaks were such a big deal For the first time financial authorities and regular citizens alike had complete transparency of the structures that had been set up by some of the wealthiest people in the world Again while none of this was illegal by itself it’s pretty clear that someone putting this much time effort and money into making such a complex and opaque international business structure is not doing it just for asset protection or business operations There is a common trend that was found amongst most of the more questionable leaked files The operating businesses were usually based in countries with less than stellar records with corruption the money from them would then be transferred to holding companies that operated in much more politically stable jurisdictions London City Singapore and the Netherlands were all very popular choices It’s not worth going to all of this effort to hide and secure your assets if they just get seized in some political revolution or economic meltdown These holding companies in these stable countries would then be owned by a string of trusts and companies before ultimately been fed back to their owner in whatever country they lived in So has anything actually been done about this Well yes a few big things actually It is easy to get disheartened about all of this rampart corruption and tax dodging going unpunished but the information revealed in the Panama Papers and other subsequent leaks has led to the arrest of dozens of high profile officials the resignation of a prime minister and the return of hundreds of billions of dollars to tax agencies all over the world The second thing it did was introduce widely recognized standards for registered companies to list beneficial owners If you try to set up a new business today in most countries around the world a major question you will get asked is who are the beneficial owners A beneficial owner is the natural person that receives the profits from the business at the end of everything The need for it to be a natural person means that the endless cobweb of shell companies does nothing because you still need to list an actual person at the end of it all The third thing it did was heightened the scrutiny placed on certain individuals known in the industry as PEP’s or Politically Exposed Persons If the beneficial owner of a company is someone who holds public office or a senior position in a large company they are liable to be involved in corruption It’s because of this that new international banking laws require that these individuals declare themselves when doing so much as opening a bank account This means that countries know where to start when auditing new companies minimizing the chances that these individuals can hide their ill-gotten gains The final major thing is the push for a global minimum tax As I was creating this video Ireland a famous destination international corporate structures agreed to implement a 15 corporate tax rate as part of the global minimum tax rate proposal This scheme would likely not have nearly the momentum it has today if it weren’t for these leaks exposing just how big this issue was It’s easy to get disheartened by people saying that nothing will ever come of this but that apathy is exactly what these fraudulent operations want If people think nothing will come of these reports then people stop caring about the reports if people stop caring about the reports then media outlets won’t publish them and if media outlets won’t publish them then they will never by investigated in the first place Now if you were thinking throughout this entire video that if you can’t beat them join them I like your style go and watch my video on what to do if you get rich so that you too can be an internationally condemned businessman As always thank you to my channel members and patron on Patreon for making it possible for everybody to keep learning How Money Works

of multiple holding companies which are each in a country with strong corporate privacy
laws.

in turn held by another foreign holding company they would need to ring up the business regulator
from the country where that other holding company is domiciled and ask them for details
on that companies ownership structure.

authorities are likely to just get told to go duck themselves because local laws mean
that kind of information is kept secret.
You can start to see the problem here, and you can start to see why these data leaks
were such a big deal.
For the first time financial authorities and regular citizens alike had complete transparency
of the structures that had been set up by some of the wealthiest people in the world.
Again while none of this was illegal by itself, it’s pretty clear that someone putting this
much time, effort and money into making such a complex and opaque international business
structure is not doing it just for asset protection or business operations.
There is a common trend that was found amongst most of the more questionable leaked files.
The operating businesses were usually based in countries with less than stellar records
with corruption, the money from them would then be transferred to holding companies that
operated in much more politically stable jurisdictions.
London City, Singapore, and the Netherlands were all very popular choices.

get seized in some political revolution or economic meltdown.

and companies before ultimately been fed back to their owner in whatever country they lived
in.

developers were able to buy up more 70 year leases and build more houses regular investors were able to get access to properties that were far cheaper than existing apartments for sale in china and less interconnected with American markets than say American markets are with European markets What’s more is that it’s hard to believe that the Chinese government would let it get quiet that bad The strength and unfaltering growth of the Economy has been the linchpin of the current government If they were to loose that they would not only have to deal with an economic catastrophe but also this video please consider liking and subscribing for new video’s like this one made every week Ok so there are three really interesting and unique ways these major wars have been funded over the past 2 decades that this game has existed But let’s start with the most basic one The game is home to a selection of megacorporations that are run entirely by players similar in many ways to guilds in world of warcraft only on a much larger scale Now the largest of these corporations effectively run like nation states they have defined borders a standing military taxation industry and of course command structures These large institutions will inevitably but heads with other similar entities over resources territory or you know just for fun At the end of the day it is a video game so the ships funded out of the money they make in game themselves But if these ships are lost in battle the mega corporations will pay to replace them They do this because ultimately they will need manpower to win these wars Ensuring that people aren’t too afraid of losing their ships will mean that their players will keep on logging in and yoloing into these devastating space battles Now these Ship Replacement Programs or SRP will most often be funded by the taxes collected from these corporations during times of relative peace The industrialist get given a safe and secure piece of territory to conduct their business and in turn they need to pay a portion of their profits to a central authority which will then fund a military program to maintain or potentially even expand this protected territory Effectively it’s exactly the same as what happens with every government ever in the real world Now this is fine in theory but often times these industrial entities don’t have the capacity to wage war themselves In these circumstances they can call on mercenary entities that do nothing but wage war on other people’s behalf for a fee Again not overly dissimilar to what happens from time to time in the real world with military contract corporations like academi performing a very similar function Now so far we have been looking at relatively minor wars the ones that might be a big deal to spectacular but that does not mean they are any less interesting Now shortly following this war the developers of EVE online decided to put an end to these player run Casino’s Now they said they had their own reasons but most players speculate it was a combination of wanting to cut down on the trade of in game money for real money and also as a response to player backlash over these entities having too much power over the game What this meant was that in 2020 there was a new funding model required The old belligerents from the casino war were ready to go at it again only this time a few factors individually, but where I think they get really interesting is when they merge together.
For a game about spaceships set 21,000 years in the future, EVE is surprisingly realistic, and
that realism extends to these massive wars in the sense that they are expensive.
The in game currency called ISK has an approximate exchange rate of about $6 per billion in game isk.
Although it must be mentioned that trading this in game currency directly back or forth for real
life money is actually against the rules of the game for now at least and will get you banned.
Even still, this shows that in game assets have a very tangible real world value on the grey market,
so when you see headlines about trillions of ISK been lost in these epic battles
it gives you an idea of just how expensive it can be to wage entire wars in EVE Online.
But this all begs a bigger question…
Who or what funds these wars?
With a price tag of hundreds of thousands of real world dollars and nothing but virtual
space pride in return, it doesn’t sound like a very good deal… Right?
Well, it’s time to learn how space money works, if you enjoy this video
please consider liking and subscribing for new video’s like this one made every week.
Ok so there are three really interesting and unique ways these major wars have been
funded over the past 2 decades that this game has existed. But let’s start with the most basic one.
The game is home to a selection of megacorporations that are run entirely
by players, similar in many ways to… guilds in world of warcraft, only on a much larger scale.
Now the largest of these corporations effectively run like nation states, they have defined borders,
a standing military, taxation, industry and of course command structures.
These large institutions will inevitably but heads with other similar entities over resources,
territory, or you know just for fun. At the end of the day it is a video game
so the reasons to go to war can simply be to entertain the members of these corporations.
Now what will normally happen is that the individual participants in these wars will need
to provide their own combat ships, funded out of the money they make in game themselves.
But if these ships are lost in battle the mega corporations will pay to replace them.
They do this because ultimately they will need manpower to win these wars.
Ensuring that people aren’t too afraid of losing their ships will mean that
their players will keep on logging in and yoloing into these devastating space battles.
Now these Ship Replacement Programs, or SRP will most often be funded by the taxes
collected from these corporations during times of relative peace.
The industrialist get given a safe and secure piece of territory to conduct their business
and in turn they need to pay a portion of their profits to a central authority which
will then fund a military program to maintain or potentially even expand this protected territory.
Effectively it’s exactly the same as what happens with every government ever in the real world.
Now this is fine in theory, but often times these industrial entities don’t have the
capacity to wage war themselves. In these circumstances they can call on mercenary
entities that do nothing but wage war on other people’s behalf for a fee.
Again not overly dissimilar to what happens from time to time in the real
world with military contract corporations like academi performing a very similar function.
Now so far we have been looking at relatively minor wars, the ones that might be a big deal
to the players of the game and s___posters on R/EVE (Pronounced AR Slash EVE) but are
not exactly that remarkable to an uninvolved onlooker like you or I.
But this all changed around 5 years ago.
You see EVE’s economy is so realistic and
so diverse that at one point there were virtual casino’s in the game…
these were founded, funded and operated entirely by regular players using the in game currency.
Of course, these casino’s generated massive profits just like most of them do in the real
world. Now these in game profits were great and all but there wasn’t much that they could
do with them on an individual level. That kind of money could buy every spaceship
in the game many times over so they needed something grander to put their money towards.
The logical answer was to sell the in game money for real world money
whether it was allowed or not. Sure they risked getting banned from a video game
but the collective total of ISK that these casino’s generated was worth millions of dollars,
so that was a risk a lot of these casino owners were willing to take.
This was especially convenient given that the thousands of transactions the
casino’s handled daily were the perfect cover from in game money laundering.
It was almost impossible to distinguish between transactions that were legitimate
and those that weren’t. Again very similar to casino’s in the real world
which are continually in the news for being centre’s for money laundering.
However the more “honourable” casino owners, decided to use their space dollars to buy
something not available on the public market… Influence.
2016 kicked off the so called Casino Wars, as the “I Want ISK”
Online Casino funded a coalition of player corporations to wage war on the single most
powerful player corporation in the game which had wronged the casino in a previous business deal.
In reality all of these other player run organisations were looking for
any excuse to go to war in an attempt to bring the “imperium” as it is known in check. They
simply lacked the financial backing to undertake such a significant challenge.
But with the casino’s writing the cheques (as a way to prove a point as to what happens when you
dishonour a business deal) one of the most devastating wars in the game’s history was
enabled which in turn gave us the PC gamer articles about spectacular space battles.
And yes, the finances behind it might be a little bit less spectacular,
but that does not mean they are any less interesting.
Now shortly following this war the developers
of EVE online decided to put an end to these player run Casino’s.
Now they said they had their own reasons but most players speculate it was a combination
of wanting to cut down on the trade of in game money for real money, and also
as a response to player backlash over these entities having too much power over the game.
What this meant was that in 2020 there was a new funding model required.
The old belligerents from the casino war were ready to go at it again,
only this time a few things were different.
For starters the casino’s were no more, which meant that no side would have
limitless funding given to them. What’s more is that 2020 was a year of working from home
with no options for entertainment besides sitting in front of a computer playing video games.
This was all shaping up to create potentially the largest conflict in the game’s history,
a conflict that would also be the most costly.
The most crucial battles during this conflict were inevitably going
to be decided by who could bring more of the largest ships in the game to bear, the titans.
These ships are extremely powerful, and were at least up until recently extremely rare,
but changes in the game in recent years had meant that the industrial powerhouses
could produce these once legendary ship’s as if they were ford model t’s.
This didn’t mean they were any less expensive however,
it just meant the powers that be had to bring more of them to keep up with their opposition.
The side that had previously been funded by the casino’s were happy to just fund
this war in the traditional way, using the tax money they had collected over
the years of peace and prosperity to foot the bill for these battles.
But the imperium had a better idea, they had seen how finance had decided their fate in 2016,
and were keen to ensure they were economically dominant going into
the war of 2020. So they once again looked to reality for inspiration.
War bonds are often issued by governments during periods of all out conflict.
This is because modern wars are expensive, and raising taxes
is often impossible if the entire economy has been dedicated towards the war effort.
So government bonds are issued so that people can invest in their own nation’s victory.
The imperium did exactly this, they sold off a series of bonds,
that would pay interest to their own members.
This was obviously great for the imperium itself because it got the
much needed injection of capital it needed to go off and fight the war,
but it was also great for the members of the group as well.
Scams, and financial fraud are commonplace in eve
and there is no regulation around taking someone’s stuff and never giving it back.
In fact these types of swindles are probably the thing that eve is third best known for.
But while having a totally unregulated financial system is
great for cool stories it’s terrible for investing,
because well anything you invest can and likely will just be stolen off you, so why bother.
These war bonds presented an opportunity for players to
invest in an asset that didn’t have quiet the same risk of being stolen.
For clarity, the imperium would be fully within their right’s to turn around and
tell these investors to get stuffed, but the hit to their entities reputation would likely
not be worth it, especially if they ever wanted to sell war bonds again to fund future wars.
Now that doesn’t mean that these in game financial instruments are totally without risk, if the
imperium get’s destroyed in this ongoing war, well then, these bonds aren’t going to get paid.
In the real world analysts call this sovereign risk,
and it’s no less important here as it is in the land of internet spaceships.
But for now at least this war is still ongoing and is likely to provide gaming magazines and
aspiring youtube channels alike many more things to talk about, like the fact that
this games financial market predicted the short squeeze on Gamestop, so make sure to like and
subscribe if you want to see us make a video on that, and in the meantime go and watch our video
to find out if the world bank is really an evil empire. Thanks for learning, How Money Works.

later on If you're a creator looking to level up your production without blowing your budget

all bad news As Q1 earnings have been revealed some brands have actually increased their sales

9% compared to last year This success has been attributed almost exclusively to the company's
Lux Boxes which have become what fast food used to be a large quantity of food with a lot of
calories for not very much money Even though the industry declined overall Taco Bell grew because
it attracted customers priced out of other options The company's own CEO boasted on the
earnings call that the company's performance was thanks to massive wins with lowincome consumers
Young Brands which also owns chains like KFC and Pizza Hut does not invest heavily into real estate
like McDonald's and instead rents most of their locations from third party commercial landlords
This means that when picking a location to open a store they don't have to worry about
the underlying fundamentals of the area in the real estate market They can focus exclusively on
what locations are going to bring in the most foot traffic This also lets brands operate in locations
